name: Michel Platini
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1978 Coupe de France with AS Nancy (scoring the winning goal in the final) and represented France at the 1978 World Cup, establishing himself as one of the country's top footballers by age 23.
early_history_summary: Platini joined the reserve side of AS Nancy in September 1972 and made his Ligue 1 debut at age 17 in May 1973. He became a regular during the 1974-75 season in Ligue 2, helping Nancy earn promotion. He won the Coupe de France with Nancy in 1978 before transferring to Saint-Étienne in 1979, where he continued to dominate French football.
primary_leverage_engine: Early specialization with family domain access
family_context_summary: Born to Aldo and Anna Platini in Jœuf, Lorraine, a family of Italian immigrant ancestry. His father Aldo was an amateur footballer, coach, and long-time sporting director for AS Nancy, the club where Michel began his professional career.
parent_family_domain_summary: Aldo Platini was a footballer, coach, and sporting director at AS Nancy, providing Michel with direct access to professional football from childhood. Aldo also created the football school at AS Jœuf where Michel first trained.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father footballer, Nancy access, domain proximity, Italian immigrant community
evidence_summary: Platini's father Aldo was a professional footballer and long-time sporting director at AS Nancy, giving Michel direct entry to professional football. He joined Nancy's reserve team at 17 and debuted in Ligue 1 in 1973. Despite failing a medical at Metz due to breathing difficulties, he developed into one of France's best players, winning the 1978 Coupe de France with Nancy and playing at the 1978 World Cup. His family's deep football connections provided unusual domain proximity from childhood, though the family was of modest means.

name: Enrico Bombieri
milestone_by_age_26: Appointed full professor of mathematics at the University of Cagliari in 1965 at age 25, and awarded the Caccioppoli Prize in 1966 for his contributions to analytic number theory, including the Bombieri mean value theorem on prime distribution.
early_history_summary: Bombieri published his first mathematical paper at age 16 in 1957. He earned his Laurea in mathematics from the University of Milan at 22 in 1963 under Giovanni Ricci, then studied at Trinity College, Cambridge with Harold Davenport. He became an assistant professor at Cagliari in 1963 and was promoted to full professor by 1965, later moving to the University of Pisa in 1966.
family_context_summary: Born in Milan to a wealthy family; his father was CEO of the Banca Commerciale Italiana. The family also owned a vineyard in Montepulciano. Bombieri is described as the fourth child and only son of a banker.
parent_family_domain_summary: Bombieri's father was a prominent banker (CEO of Banca Commerciale Italiana), not a mathematician, but the family's wealth and social position provided access to elite education and intellectual freedom from an early age.
primary_early_advantage_tags: math prodigy, wealthy family, University of Milan, Trinity College Cambridge, Giovanni Ricci
evidence_summary: Bombieri was a mathematical prodigy who read algebra at age 8, studied number theory at 13, and published his first paper at 16. His father was CEO of Banca Commerciale Italiana, providing financial security and access to elite education. He earned his Laurea at the University of Milan under Giovanni Ricci, then studied at Trinity College, Cambridge with Harold Davenport. By 25 he was a full professor at Cagliari, and by 26 he had won the Caccioppoli Prize. His extraordinary early mathematical ability combined with institutional access and financial safety to enable rapid academic advancement.

name: Ayrton Senna
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first Formula One Grand Prix at the 1985 Portuguese GP (age 25), having already won the British and European Formula Ford championships (1981), British F3 Championship and Macau Grand Prix (1983), and debuted in F1 with Toleman in 1984 scoring multiple podiums.
early_history_summary: Senna began competitive kart racing at age 13 in 1973, using a go-kart built by his father. He was twice runner-up at the Karting World Championship (1979, 1980). He moved to England in 1981 to race Formula Ford 1600, winning the British and European championships. He dominated Formula Ford 2000 in 1982, won the British F3 Championship in 1983, and entered F1 with Toleman in 1984 before moving to Lotus in 1985 where he took his first pole and victory.
family_context_summary: Born to a wealthy Brazilian family in São Paulo. His father Milton Guirado da Silva was a landowner and factory owner who operated a metallurgical company (Universal) supplying auto manufacturers, with additional investments in construction, farms, and livestock. Senna was the middle child of three.
parent_family_domain_summary: Senna's father Milton owned a metallurgical company supplying the automotive industry and built Ayrton's first go-kart using a lawnmower engine. The family's wealth funded Ayrton's early karting career and supported his move to European racing, though Milton initially hoped Ayrton would join the family business.
primary_early_advantage_tags: wealthy family, father automotive factory, go-kart at age 4, karting from 13, Brazilian motorsport
evidence_summary: Senna was born into a wealthy São Paulo family; his father Milton owned a metallurgical company supplying the automotive industry and built Ayrton's first go-kart at age 4. Senna started competitive karting at 13, was twice World Championship runner-up, then dominated British Formula Ford and F3 before entering F1 at 24. His father's wealth funded his early racing career, and the family's automotive business provided direct domain proximity. His natural driving talent was evident from his first kart race, where he started on pole against older drivers.

name: Nadia Comăneci
milestone_by_age_26: Scored the first perfect 10.0 in Olympic gymnastics history at the 1976 Montreal Games at age 14, winning three Olympic gold medals (all-around, uneven bars, balance beam), a silver, and a bronze. She went on to win World Championship golds in 1978-79 and two more Olympic golds in 1980.
early_history_summary: Comăneci was discovered by Béla Károlyi at age 6 when he spotted her turning cartwheels in a schoolyard in Onești, Romania. She entered her first competition at 7, won the Romanian National Junior Championship at 9, and won three golds at her first international junior meet in 1972. By 1975 she was senior European champion, and at 14 she made Olympic history in Montreal.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and extreme early specialization
family_context_summary: Born to Gheorghe (an auto mechanic) and Ștefania Comăneci in Onești, a small industrial town in the Carpathian Mountains. Her parents separated in the 1970s. The family was working class; Nadia's gymnastics training was funded through the Romanian state sports system.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to gymnastics; Comăneci was discovered by coach Béla Károlyi at age 6 in a schoolyard. Her success was driven by the Romanian state gymnastics pipeline rather than family domain advantage.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Karolyi coaching from age 6, Romanian state gymnastics, prodigy, perfect 10 at 14, Cold War sports
evidence_summary: Comăneci was discovered at age 6 by Béla Károlyi, who built an experimental gymnastics school in Onești. She trained intensively (8 hours/day, 6 days/week from age 12) within the Romanian state sports system. Her working-class family had no gymnastics background; her father was an auto mechanic. Károlyi's sustained, individualized coaching from age 6 and the state-funded gymnastics pipeline were the dominant early advantages. Her natural physical talent was evident from the start, and her extraordinary composure at age 14 produced the first perfect 10 in Olympic history.

name: Tom Jones
milestone_by_age_26: His second single 'It's Not Unusual' reached #1 on the UK Singles Chart in March 1965 (age 24) and #10 on the US Billboard Hot 100, launching him to international fame. He followed with 'What's New Pussycat?' (1965) and other hits before age 26.
early_history_summary: Born Thomas John Woodward in Treforest, Wales, Jones sang from childhood at family gatherings and in school choir. He married at 16 and worked manual jobs (construction, glove factory, paper mill) while singing in Welsh clubs at night. In 1963 he became frontman of Tommy Scott and the Senators, was discovered by manager Gordon Mills, signed to Decca, and released 'It's Not Unusual' in early 1965.
family_context_summary: Born to Freda Jones and Thomas Woodward, a coal miner, in Treforest, Wales. He was diagnosed with tuberculosis at age 12 and spent two years bedridden. He married at 16 and worked manual jobs to support his young family before finding success as a singer.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to music or entertainment. His father was a coal miner. Jones's singing talent was nurtured informally through Welsh community traditions and school choir, not through family domain expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: coal miner's son, TB at 12, married at 16, Welsh singing tradition, Gordon Mills manager, 1960s pop boom
evidence_summary: Jones was born into a working-class Welsh mining family with no music industry connections. He contracted TB at 12, was bedridden for two years listening to music, married at 16, and worked manual jobs while singing in clubs at night. His powerful natural voice was recognized from childhood, but his breakthrough came when manager Gordon Mills discovered him performing with the Senators in 1963 and secured a Decca deal. The 1960s pop music boom and Mills's songwriting partnership propelled 'It's Not Unusual' to #1 in 1965. His path was defined by adversity and self-creation rather than inherited advantage.

name: James Hunt
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Formula One debut at the 1973 Monaco Grand Prix with Hesketh Racing (age 25) and scored podium finishes at the Dutch and US Grands Prix in his rookie season, establishing himself as a rising F1 talent by age 26. He had previously won races in Formula Ford and Formula Three.
early_history_summary: Hunt discovered motor racing at age 18 when he attended a club meeting at Silverstone. He began racing a Mini in 1967, working odd jobs to fund his career after his parents refused to support him. He moved to Formula Ford in 1968, won races, then graduated to Formula Three in 1969 where he earned the nickname 'Hunt the Shunt' for his aggressive style. Lord Hesketh signed him in 1973, entering F1 with a March chassis.
family_context_summary: Born in Belmont, Surrey, the son of Wallis Glynn Gunthorpe Hunt, a London stockbroker, and Susan Noel Wentworth Hunt. He was educated at Wellington College, a public school. Despite the middle-class background, his parents refused to support his racing ambitions, forcing him to fund his own career through odd jobs.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to motorsport. His father was a stockbroker and the family was middle class. The family's refusal to fund James's racing meant he was entirely self-funded in his early career, buying a crashed Mini and rebuilding it himself.
primary_early_advantage_tags: stockbroker father, self-funded racing, Lord Hesketh patron, Wellington College, UK motorsport, Hunt the Shunt
evidence_summary: Hunt was the son of a London stockbroker and attended Wellington College, but his parents refused to support his racing ambitions. He funded his own career through odd jobs, buying and rebuilding a crashed Mini to begin racing at 20. He progressed through Formula Ford and Formula Three, earning a reputation for both speed and crashes ('Hunt the Shunt'). Lord Hesketh's patronage in 1973 lifted him into Formula One, where he scored podiums in his rookie season at 25. His path was defined by self-creation against family resistance rather than inherited advantage, though his English public school background and the UK's central role in motorsport provided structural context.

name: Carla Bruni
milestone_by_age_26: By age 24 (1992), Bruni was among the 20 highest-paid fashion models in the world, modeling for Christian Dior, Chanel, Versace, Yves Saint-Laurent, Givenchy, and Karl Lagerfeld, earning approximately $1 million per year. She signed with City Models at 19 in 1987 and rose rapidly through the Guess? campaign and major runway shows.
early_history_summary: Bruni was born in Turin to a wealthy industrialist family (CEAT tire fortune). The family relocated to France in the early 1970s to escape Red Brigades kidnapping threats. She attended a Swiss boarding school, then studied art and architecture in Paris. At 19, her brother's girlfriend suggested she try modeling; she signed with City Models and was chosen by Paul Marciano for the Guess? jeans campaign, launching her to top-model status within a few years.
family_context_summary: Born to Alberto Bruni Tedeschi, an industrialist and classical composer who was heir to the CEAT tire manufacturing fortune, and Marisa Borini, a concert pianist. The family was very wealthy, owning castles and art collections. They moved from Turin to France in the early 1970s to escape Red Brigades kidnapping threats targeting wealthy Italian families.
parent_family_domain_summary: Bruni's father was an industrialist (CEAT tire company director) and classical composer; her mother was a concert pianist. The family's immense wealth, social position in Italian high society, and cultural sophistication provided direct access to the fashion and arts world, though not specifically to modeling.
primary_early_advantage_tags: CEAT tire heiress, wealthy family, Swiss boarding school, Paris fashion, Guess? campaign, 1990s supermodel era
evidence_summary: Bruni was born into one of Italy's wealthiest families as heiress to the CEAT tire fortune. Her father was an industrialist and composer; her mother a concert pianist. The family relocated to France to escape kidnapping threats, and Carla attended a Swiss boarding school before studying art in Paris. At 19, she signed with City Models and was quickly chosen for the Guess? campaign, which launched her to the top tier of 1990s fashion modeling. By 24, she was among the 20 highest-paid models, earning about $1 million annually. Her family's wealth, social capital, and proximity to Parisian high society provided a platform that made entry into elite modeling far more accessible.

name: Krešimir Ćosić
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic silver medal with Yugoslavia at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics at age 19, followed by World Championship gold in 1970 (age 22), EuroBasket MVP in 1971 (age 23), and another Olympic silver in 1972 (age 24). He was a collegiate All-American at BYU and a 6× FIBA European Selection player by age 26.
early_history_summary: Ćosić was born in Zagreb and raised in Zadar, where he started playing basketball at age 16 in 1964. He quickly became a star for KK Zadar, winning Yugoslav League championships in 1965, 1967, and 1968. He played for Yugoslavia at the 1968 Olympics (silver medal) before attending BYU from 1970-1973, where he was a three-time first-team All-WAC selection and All-American. He returned to Zadar after college and continued his dominant national team career.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and elite performance pipeline
family_context_summary: Born to Ante and Darinka Ćosić in Zagreb, Yugoslavia (now Croatia). He was raised in Zadar. Family financial background is not documented in reviewed sources; he grew up in communist Yugoslavia where sports were state-supported.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to basketball is documented in reviewed sources. Ćosić's path to basketball appears to have been driven by his exceptional height (6'11") and the Yugoslav state sports system rather than family domain expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Yugoslav national team, 6'11" height, Zadar basketball, BYU, Olympic silver at 19, World Championship gold
evidence_summary: Ćosić was born in Zagreb and raised in Zadar, where he began playing basketball at 16. His exceptional 6'11" height was a decisive physical advantage. The Yugoslav state sports system provided an elite performance pipeline: he won Yugoslav League titles with Zadar as a teenager, earned an Olympic silver medal at 19 in 1968, then attended BYU on a basketball scholarship where he became an All-American. Family background is not well documented, but his path was driven by the state sports system, his extraordinary physical attributes, and the rising Yugoslav basketball program rather than inherited advantage.
